title: Knowledge check: Using the R Console

questions.prompt: For “Using the R Console”, which approach best supports a reliable result?
options: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
Trust the first output without inspecting its inputs.
Hide warnings and skip validation to make the result look clean.
Change several unrelated parts at once so the cause of any result is unclear.
questions.answer_key: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
questions.explanation: Using the R Console is one step in R Syntax and Fundamental Rules; r is case-sensitive. Assignment creates or replaces objects; expressions evaluate to values even when they are not explicitly printed. Reliable work makes assumptions visible and checks behavior before scaling up.

questions.prompt: Which item is explicitly listed under “Using the R Console” in the source curriculum?
options: Change unrelated settings before checking the input
Assume one example proves every edge case
Skip validation when the output looks plausible
questions.explanation: The source PDF lists “Interactive Execution” as part of lesson 13. The lesson retains the original topic wording.

questions.prompt: When applying “Using the R Console” to real work, what should you do before relying on the result?
options: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
Assume missing and malformed inputs never occur.
Use the same method regardless of data type or the research question.
Remove inconvenient observations without recording the decision.
questions.answer_key: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
questions.explanation: Run examples line by line and inspect the global environment only as a debugging aid. Record assumptions and known limitations instead of presenting a demonstration as proof.
